children: Startup equity can look like a lucrative trade for accepting a below-market salary, but the eventual payout can be dramatically smaller than the headline stake suggests, according to Nick Maggiulli of Of Dollars And Data.

Maggiulli showed the gap with a hypothetical employee who receives a 0.25% stake in a startup and expects to make $250,000 if the company sells for $100M. After accounting for how startup equity typically works, however, he calculated that the initial grant would be worth $97,500 rather than $250,000.

The difference comes from factors that can reduce the value of an employee's equity before an exit, including vesting, dilution, liquidation preferences, exercise costs, and taxes. A typical four-year vesting schedule means an employee who leaves after two years would receive only half of the original grant, while subsequent funding rounds can further reduce the ownership stake.

The biggest risk may be whether a startup exits at all. Maggiulli cited data showing that only 30% of 1,119 U.S. seed companies tracked by CB Insights had an exit, while he estimated that 70% of startups do not produce a liquidity event.

For his hypothetical early employee, Maggiulli estimated a 25% chance of a small exit, a 4% chance of a big exit, and a 1% chance of a unicorn exit, alongside the 70% probability of no exit. Under those assumptions, he calculated
the employee's expected payout across all outcomes at $35,820

That expected payout would also arrive years in the future and would have to compensate for the risk, the time required to vest, and any salary discount accepted to join the startup. Maggiulli noted that an employee taking $20,000 less than market pay each year would forgo $80,000 of income over four years, or $48,000 after his assumed tax rate.

The calculation also does not account for every way startup equity can become less valuable. Maggiulli said liquidation preferences or discounting future payouts to present value could reduce the expected value further, while leaving before an exit and being unable to afford the exercise cost could result in a zero payout.

title: Here's the payout the average startup employee can expect
